summary:
Numbers opens in the Wilderness of Sinai in the second year after the exodus (1:1) and ends on the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho. The English title, from the Greek and Latin versions, refers to the two censuses — head counts of men of fighting age — that frame the book: 603,550 at Sinai (1:46), 601,730 on the plains of Moab (26:51). The Hebrew title covers everything in between: bemidbar, "in the wilderness." Totals that size imply well over two million people; some scholars read the Hebrew eleph, usually "thousand," as a clan or fighting unit in these lists, yielding smaller totals, while others take the figures at face value. The text does not settle it.

Chapters 1–10 are ordered preparation: the tribes camped in formation around the tabernacle (the tent sanctuary), the Levites — the tribe set apart to carry and guard it — assigned their duties, and the priests taught a blessing to speak over Israel: "May the LORD bless you and keep you" (6:24). The march begins in chapter 10 and the complaining in chapter 11 — about food, hardship, and Moses himself. The break comes at Kadesh (13–14): twelve spies scout Canaan for forty days, ten report fortified cities and people of such size that "We seemed like grasshoppers in our own sight" (13:33), and the people resolve to choose a new leader and return to Egypt; only Joshua and Caleb dissent. The sentence: "In keeping with the forty days you spied out the land, you shall bear your guilt forty years" (14:34) — the counted generation, twenty years old and up, will die in the wilderness. Deuteronomy 1:2 notes that the journey from Horeb (Sinai) to Kadesh takes eleven days.

The forty years pass in few chapters. Korah leads a revolt against Moses and Aaron, and "the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them" (16:32). At Meribah, Moses strikes the rock he was told to speak to and is barred from the land himself (20:12). When venomous snakes strike the camp, Moses is told to mount a serpent on a pole: "If anyone who was bitten looked at the bronze snake, he would live" (21:9). Jesus points back to that scene: "Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up" (John 3:14).

King Balak of Moab then hires Balaam, a seer from the Euphrates, to curse Israel (22–24). Balaam's donkey sees the angel of the LORD before the seer does, and speaks (22:22–30); every attempted curse comes out as blessing, among them "A star will come forth from Jacob, and a scepter will arise from Israel" (24:17), a line later Jewish and Christian readers took as pointing to a coming ruler. Israel then joins in worshiping Baal of Peor with the women of Moab, and a plague kills 24,000 (25:9). The second census finds "not one who had been numbered by Moses and Aaron" at Sinai still alive except Caleb and Joshua (26:64–65). Joshua is commissioned as Moses' successor (27:18–23), the daughters of Zelophehad win the right to inherit when a father dies without sons (27:1–11; 36), and the book ends at the border: "on the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho" (36:13).
